claims.text: Rapid solidification, such as melt spinning, will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to a conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys have relatively coarse lamellar or dual-phase microstructures.
Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys typically have high strength.
Their high strength is attributable to second-phase strengthening.
Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys typically suffer from poor ductility associated with cleavage fracture.
Stress localization contributes to the poor ductility of coarse eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Rapid solidification will drastically reduce eutectic interlamellar spacing.
Rapid solidification will improve the distribution of phases.
Reduced interlamellar spacing produces a higher density of interfaces between phases.
Lamellar or grain refinement raises yield strength through Hall–Petch-type interlamellar or grain-boundary strengthening.
Improved strain distribution at refined interfaces delays crack initiation and propagation.
Delayed crack initiation and propagation enhance ductility.
Rapidly solidified material will have greater yield strength than the as-cast or conventionally processed baseline.
Rapidly solidified material will have greater elongation to failure than the as-cast or conventionally processed baseline.
The refined microstructure will produce more uniform plastic deformation and greater resistance to crack propagation.
The beneficial effect should hold in eutectic high-entropy alloys having similar compositions and phase structures when rapid solidification significantly changes lamellar spacing.
The beneficial effect may fail when processing does not achieve microstructural refinement or when alloy thermodynamics are unfavorable for controlled phase separation.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends sensitively on cooling rate and resulting lamellar dimensions.
